Week one. Vikas's app launch, the one he'd championed for a year, crashed on day one. In the meeting, his colleagues said, 'Tough luck,' and 'These things happen.' But Sangeeta caught his eye across the table and there was a small, bright smile she didn't quite hide.

Week two. Vikas heard laughter from the pantry and his project name in it. When he walked in, it stopped. 'Hey, Vikas!' Everyone was very polite.

Week four. He ate lunch at his desk every day now. He'd stopped suggesting ideas in meetings. His sister asked on the phone why he sounded so flat. 'It's not that it failed,' he said. 'It's that some of them seem to be enjoying it.' He felt very small saying it aloud.

qa.a: For a year.

qa.a: Vikas feels lonely and small, eating alone and hurt that some colleagues seem to enjoy his failure.

qa.q: What could help Vikas now?
qa.a: He could talk to a manager or a trusted colleague about the atmosphere, and keep sharing his feelings with his sister rather than withdrawing.

qa.q: What might Sangeeta's small smile show about her?
qa.a: It may show envy or a sense of relief that his big project failed, even while she stayed polite.

grounding: A colleague whose project failed senses smiles behind polite words and feels lonely and small.

subtype: Person whose failure is enjoyed [Receiver]
passage: Chaitanya, you're worried the team will laugh because your pitch failed? Let your Gurpreet Mausi tell you a story. When I was twenty-five, I led the first computer project in our Amritsar bank branch, 1995. On launch day, the whole system froze. Customers queued out of the door. My colleagues said kind things to my face. But I saw them smile at each other when they thought I wasn't looking. I heard one say, 'Madam wanted to be modern.' That sting was worse than the failure. I went home and cried in the bathroom so my children wouldn't hear. The next week, one senior, Mr Bedi, sat with me and asked what we'd learned. Only him. That one kindness is why I stayed.

qa.q: In which year did the bank's computer project fail?
How did Gurpreet feel when she saw colleagues smiling at each other?
qa.a: Gurpreet felt stung and humiliated, more hurt by their enjoyment than by the failure itself.

qa.q: Which choice inside the story helped Gurpreet most, and why?
qa.a: Mr Bedi sitting with her to ask what they'd learned, because one sincere kindness countered the sting of others' glee.

qa.q: How might Mr Bedi have seen the failed launch?
qa.a: Mr Bedi seems to have seen it as a learning moment, not a chance to mock.

grounding: An elder recalls how colleagues' hidden enjoyment of her failed project stung more than the failure, and how one kindness helped.

subtype: Person whose failure is enjoyed [Receiver]
passage: Trisha had forty minutes to pack up her stall before the building shut. The pop-up bakery she'd pitched to the whole co-working space had sold eleven cupcakes in two days. As she stacked the unsold boxes, Gurleen from the next desk came by. 'Oh no,' Gurleen said, but her eyes were bright, and she glanced back at her friends by the window, who were grinning. 'Maybe next time,' someone called. Trisha smiled and said, 'Maybe.' Her hands shook as she taped the boxes. It wasn't the eleven cupcakes. It was the grins. On the bus home, with the rain hammering the windows, she felt tiny and very alone. She texted her flatmate: 'Can you just be home tonight?'

qa.q: How many cupcakes did Trisha sell in two days?
qa.a: Eleven.

qa.q: What made Trisha feel tiny and alone?
qa.a: The grins and bright eyes of colleagues who seemed to enjoy her failure hurt more than the low sales.

qa.q: What was wise about Trisha's text to her flatmate?
qa.a: Asking for company let her share the sting with someone kind instead of carrying it alone.

qa.q: How might Gurleen's glance at her friends affect Trisha?
qa.a: It told Trisha that her failure was being enjoyed, which made the 'Oh no' feel hollow and hurtful.

grounding: A colleague whose bakery pop-up failed senses grins behind polite words and feels lonely and small.

subtype: Noticing the pleasure without acting on it [Response]
passage:
Coach's note, badminton academy

Today Dilnaz's old rival from the state circuit lost in the first round, in front of everyone. I saw a flash on Dilnaz's face, a quick bright look, gone in a second. Afterwards she came to me and said something I respect. 'Devika, I felt happy when she lost. I'm not proud of it. I think I'm scared she'll always beat me.' She didn't post about it or tell the others. Instead she walked over to the rival and said, 'Rough match. You'll be back.' Then she asked me to add two extra practice sessions a week. Next step: I'll set her a clear plan for the backhand, which is what she fears most in that match-up.

Devika, coach

qa.q: What did Dilnaz say to her rival after the match?
qa.a: 'Rough match. You'll be back.'

qa.q: What does Dilnaz's quick, bright look suggest she was feeling?
qa.a: Dilnaz felt a quick glee mixed with fear, scared that the rival would always beat her.

qa.q: Which part of Dilnaz's response could others copy?
qa.a: Admitting the feeling privately, not broadcasting it, staying kind to the person who lost, and using the envy to plan her own practice.

qa.q: How might the rival have felt hearing Dilnaz's words?
qa.a: The rival probably felt surprised and comforted, receiving kindness at a painful moment.

grounding: An adult admits a flash of glee at a rival's loss, doesn't broadcast it, and asks what the envy points to in her own life.

subtype: Noticing the pleasure without acting on it [Response]
passage:
Tuesday

Heard today that Dilnaz's startup shut down. For one second, I felt glad. Really glad. She was the one who got the award I wanted in college, the one everyone called 'the next big thing'. I noticed the feeling and I didn't like it, but I didn't pretend it wasn't there either. I didn't tell the group chat. I didn't ask 'what happened?' with fake concern. Instead I sat with it and asked myself: what am I actually envious of? Not her failure. Her courage to try. I haven't started anything in three years. So I sent her a message: 'Heard the news. I'm sorry. That took guts.' And I opened the business plan I abandoned in 2022.

Gargi

qa.q: What had happened to Dilnaz's startup?
qa.a: It had shut down.

qa.q: What did Gargi feel on hearing the news, and what was decided about that feeling?
qa.a: Gargi felt a brief, real gladness, did not like it, and chose to notice it honestly rather than act on it.

qa.q: What did Gargi learn from asking what she envied?
qa.a: That the envy was for Dilnaz's courage to try, which pushed Gargi to reopen an abandoned business plan.

qa.q: How might Dilnaz feel receiving Gargi's message?
qa.a: Dilnaz would probably feel comforted and respected, getting kindness instead of gossip at a hard time.

grounding: An adult admits a flash of glee at another's failure, doesn't broadcast it, and asks what the envy points to in the writer's own life.

subtype: Joy at a friend's win [Actor]
passage: The prize-giving was held on the hottest day of May, and the fans in the school hall had stopped working. Wasim sat sweating in the third row. When the principal called 'Zeenat Hussain, first prize, essay writing!', Wasim clapped so hard his hands stung. Zeenat was his best friend. She'd read him her essay on the bus every day for a week. Under his clapping, though, there was a tiny pang. He had entered too, and his name wasn't called. He noticed it, like a pebble in his shoe. But when Zeenat came back holding the certificate, he grinned and said, 'Told you!' The pang was still there, a little. So was the warm, happy feeling. Both at the same time.

qa.q: Which prize did Zeenat win?
qa.a: First prize in essay writing.

qa.q: What was Wasim feeling while he clapped?
qa.a: Wasim felt warm and happy for Zeenat, with a tiny pang underneath because his own name wasn't called.

qa.q: What could a teacher say to children who feel both happy and a little sad at prize-giving?
qa.a: The teacher could say it's normal to feel both, and that being glad for a friend while wishing for yourself is okay.

qa.q: How might Zeenat feel hearing Wasim say 'Told you!'?
qa.a: Zeenat would likely feel happy and supported, knowing her friend believed in her.

grounding: A child claps hard when a friend wins a prize and feels warmth, with a small pang of wishing for himself beneath it.

passage: The Christmas term science fair at the Delhi school ended with the results. When Dhruv's name was read out for first prize, Jyoti jumped up and clapped louder than anyone. She had helped him paint the volcano. Her own project, the water filter, got a 'good effort' sticker. For a moment, walking back to her seat, she felt a pang, like a pinch. She would have liked her name to be called too. But then Dhruv ran over and hugged her. 'Your red paint won it!' Jyoti laughed, and the warm feeling was bigger than the pinch. At home she told Mumma, 'I'm so happy for Dhruv. And I want to win next year.'
